stem: What is the maximum number of interviews the linguist can have transcribed without going over budget?
stimulus: A linguist studying a regional dialect pays a transcription service to turn recorded interviews into written text. The service charges a one-time setup fee of $30 plus $12 per interview. The linguist's budget for transcription is $160.
explanation: Set up total cost ≤ budget: $12x + 30 \le 160$. Subtract 30 to get $12x \le 130$, so $x \le 10.8\overline{3}$. The number of interviews must be a whole number, and a maximum rounds down, so the answer is 10. Check: $12(10) + 30 = 150 \le 160$, but $12(11) + 30 = 162 > 160$.

B.why: You rounded $10.8\overline{3}$ up to 11. For a maximum you have to round down, because 11 interviews would cost $162, which is over the budget.

C.why: You left out the $30 setup fee and divided the whole $160 by 12 to get about 13.3, then rounded down. The fee has to come out of the budget first.

D.why: 130 is the number of dollars left after the setup fee. You still have to divide by $12 per interview to get the number of interviews.

stem: What is the minimum number of whole hours the printmaker must run the press to have at least 250 prints in total?
stimulus: A printmaker is producing a limited edition of a woodcut and has already printed 30 copies. The press produces 40 more prints per hour. The printmaker needs a total of at least 250 prints.
explanation: Set up output ≥ goal: $30 + 40h \ge 250$. Subtract 30 to get $40h \ge 220$, so $h \ge 5.5$. A minimum rounds up, so the printmaker needs 6 hours. Check: $30 + 40(6) = 270 \ge 250$, but $30 + 40(5) = 230 < 250$.

A.why: You rounded 5.5 down to 5. For a minimum you have to round up, because 5 hours gives only 230 prints, which is short of 250.

C.why: You ignored the 30 prints that were already made and divided 250 by 40 to get 6.25, then rounded up to 7. Those 30 prints count toward the total.

D.why: 220 is the number of prints still needed, not the number of hours. Divide by 40 prints per hour to finish.

stem: What is the maximum number of grid squares the cartographer can survey on the rest of this battery charge?
stimulus: A cartographer uses a drone to photograph a coastline for a new map. A full battery charge lasts 90 minutes, and the cartographer has already used 18 minutes of this charge flying to the site. Surveying one grid square takes 7 minutes of flight time.
explanation: Set up time used ≤ time available: $18 + 7s \le 90$. Subtract 18 to get $7s \le 72$, so $s \le 10.\overline{285714}$. A maximum rounds down, so the answer is 10 squares. Check: $18 + 7(10) = 88 \le 90$, but $18 + 7(11) = 95 > 90$.

B.why: You rounded about 10.3 up to 11. Eleven squares would need 95 minutes in total, which is more than the battery provides, so a maximum must round down.

C.why: You divided the full 90 minutes by 7 and got about 12.9, then rounded down. You left out the 18 minutes that were already used.

D.why: You left out the 18 minutes already used and also rounded 12.9 up. That makes two errors: the time already flown wasn't subtracted, and the maximum was rounded the wrong way.

stem: What is the maximum number of coolers the van can carry on one trip?
stimulus: A public health department uses a mobile clinic van to bring vaccines to rural communities. The van can safely carry at most 1,200 pounds. The driver, nurse, and medical equipment together weigh 260 pounds. Each cooler of vaccine weighs 45 pounds.
explanation: Set up total weight ≤ limit: $260 + 45c \le 1{,}200$. Subtract 260 to get $45c \le 940$, so $c \le 20.\overline{8}$. A maximum rounds down, so the van can carry 20 coolers. Check: $260 + 45(20) = 1{,}160 \le 1{,}200$, but $260 + 45(21) = 1{,}205 > 1{,}200$.

B.why: You rounded $20.\overline{8}$ up to 21. With 21 coolers the load is 1,205 pounds, which goes over the limit, so a maximum must round down.

C.why: You divided the whole 1,200 pounds by 45 and got about 26.7. The 260 pounds of people and equipment use up part of that capacity first.

D.why: 940 is the capacity left in pounds after the people and equipment are loaded. You still need to divide by 45 pounds per cooler.

stem: What is the minimum number of whole minutes the athlete must run so that the total number of calories burned in the session is more than 600?
stimulus: A sports scientist is monitoring an athlete's energy use during a training session. The athlete burned 160 calories during a warm-up and then runs on a treadmill, burning 11 calories per minute. The goal is for the session's total to be more than 600 calories.
explanation: "More than" is strict: $160 + 11m > 600$. Subtract 160 to get $11m > 440$, so $m > 40$. Exactly 40 minutes gives a total of exactly 600 calories, which is not more than 600, so the smallest whole number that works is 41. Check: $160 + 11(41) = 611 > 600$.

A.why: You kept the boundary value. At 40 minutes the total is exactly 600 calories, and the condition is strictly more than 600, so 40 doesn't work.

C.why: You ignored the 160 warm-up calories and divided 600 by 11 to get about 54.5, then rounded up. The warm-up already counts toward the session total.

D.why: 440 is the number of calories still needed after the warm-up, not a number of minutes. Divide by 11 calories per minute to finish.
